# Arterial Spin Labeling and Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

This chapter describes two more quantitative methods, each built on a different
piece of MR physics. Arterial spin labeling uses inflowing blood as an
endogenous tracer to measure perfusion. Quantitative susceptibility mapping uses
the phase of the signal — normally discarded — to estimate the magnetic
susceptibility of the tissue, which is sensitive to iron and myelin.

## Arterial spin labeling

Arterial spin labeling (ASL) measures cerebral blood flow (CBF) without an
injected contrast agent. The trick is to magnetically "label" arterial blood
upstream and then image the tissue after the labeled blood has arrived. Because
the label is created with an RF pulse rather than a chemical, the same
experiment can be repeated with and without labeling, and the *difference*
between the two images isolates the contribution of the delivered blood. The
labeling can be applied as a brief pulse (pulsed ASL, PASL) or as a sustained
saturation of arterial water (continuous ASL, CASL); both are usually read out
with a gradient-echo or spin-echo sequence, and background suppression is used
to remove the static signal from scalp and bone.

In continuous ASL (@fig-ch63-asl-continuous), a small dedicated coil placed near
the carotid delivers a continuous train of inversion pulses, labeling the blood
in the feeding artery. The imaging plane is then measured over time, the
measurement is repeated without labeling, and the difference reflects the
labeled spins that have flowed into the plane.

![Continuous ASL. A transmission coil near the carotid continuously labels
arterial blood; the imaging plane is measured with and without labeling, and the
difference maps the delivered blood.](images/ch63/asl-continuous.png){#fig-ch63-asl-continuous}

A widely used pulsed variant is FAIR — flow-sensitive alternating inversion
recovery (@fig-ch63-asl-fair). Here two acquisitions are compared: one labels a
thick volume around and including the imaging plane, so that spins already in
the plane plus spins flowing in both contribute; the other labels only the
plane itself. The spins in the plane contribute to both measurements, so the
difference again isolates the arterial spins that flowed in.

![FAIR (flow-sensitive alternating inversion recovery), a pulsed ASL scheme. The
difference between a non-selective and a slice-selective inversion isolates the
inflowing arterial spins.](images/ch63/asl-fair.png){#fig-ch63-asl-fair}

ASL is quantitative and physiologically specific, but it pays for that with
sensitivity. The perfusion signal change is much smaller than the BOLD signal
change measured in an ordinary functional experiment. Comparing pseudo-continuous
ASL and BOLD activation for the same task, the BOLD maps are far more robust
across subjects and sites (@fig-ch63-asl-vs-bold). ASL is chosen when an absolute,
interpretable perfusion measurement matters more than raw detection power.

![The perfusion signal change from pCASL is much smaller and less reproducible
across subjects than the BOLD signal change for the same
task.](images/ch63/asl-vs-bold.png){#fig-ch63-asl-vs-bold}

## Quantitative susceptibility mapping

Magnetic susceptibility (χ) measures how strongly a material becomes magnetized
in an applied field, χ = M/H. It is helpful to picture the material as filled
with tiny compass needles. *Paramagnetic* materials — deoxyhemoglobin, ferritin,
some neurotransmitters — weakly align with the field (χ > 0). *Diamagnetic*
materials — oxyhemoglobin, water, lipids, many proteins — weakly oppose it
(χ < 0). *Ferromagnetic* materials such as iron align strongly and can stay
aligned when the field is removed, but these are not found in the brain. Because
myelin is diamagnetic and iron-bearing molecules are paramagnetic, a map of
susceptibility carries information about both.

The complication is that susceptibility is not measured directly. What the
scanner records is the *phase* of the signal, which reflects the local field
perturbation produced by the susceptibility distribution — and that perturbation
is spatially spread out, not localized to the source. Quantitative
susceptibility mapping (QSM) begins by keeping the phase and amplitude from each
receive coil and combining them as complex numbers, rather than forming the
usual weighted sum of magnitudes (@fig-ch63-qsm-coil-combination). A naive
complex sum without phase correction can cancel to zero where the coil phases
disagree, so careful phase handling is central to the method.

![QSM retains the phase and amplitude of each coil and combines them as a complex
exponential. Without phase correction the complex sum can cancel to zero
magnitude.](images/ch63/qsm-coil-combination.png){#fig-ch63-qsm-coil-combination}

The heart of QSM is an inversion. The measured field perturbation is related to
the underlying susceptibility distribution by a known physical forward model; QSM
runs that model backward — a "field-to-source inversion" — to convert the spatial
field measurement into a spatial estimate of susceptibility. For a single
susceptibility source the field perturbation has the characteristic
dipole pattern, and the inversion recovers a compact source
(@fig-ch63-qsm-single-point). The same inversion applied voxel-by-voxel yields a
whole-brain susceptibility map (@fig-ch63-qsm-whole-brain).

![The core QSM calculation for a single source. The measured field perturbation
(a dipole pattern) is inverted through the physical forward model to estimate the
susceptibility.](images/ch63/qsm-single-point.png){#fig-ch63-qsm-single-point}

![Applying the field-to-source inversion across the whole brain produces a
susceptibility map.](images/ch63/qsm-whole-brain.png){#fig-ch63-qsm-whole-brain}

Clinically, QSM is attractive because susceptibility tracks iron deposition and
myelin loss. In multiple sclerosis, for example, the susceptibility map
delineates deep gray-matter structures and lesion cores more cleanly than the
raw phase image, whose nonlocal contrast smears the lesion edge
(@fig-ch63-qsm-multiple-sclerosis).

![QSM in multiple sclerosis. Compared with the magnitude and phase images, the
susceptibility map gives cleaner delineation of deep gray matter and a
sharper lesion core.](images/ch63/qsm-multiple-sclerosis.png){#fig-ch63-qsm-multiple-sclerosis}

A practical caution runs through the QSM literature: the inversion is
ill-posed, and there are many algorithmic choices — regularization, background
field removal, and so on — with active debate about which are correct. Community
reconstruction challenges exist precisely to compare them. It is a good place to
remember Box and Draper's aphorism that all models are wrong, but some are
useful (@fig-ch63-qsm-reconstruction-challenge).

![There are many QSM reconstruction algorithms and ongoing debate about which is
correct; community challenges compare them.](images/ch63/qsm-reconstruction-challenge.png){#fig-ch63-qsm-reconstruction-challenge}
